says: When a policy is set to Enabled, has a registry value name and defines no explicit on-value, the program writes the number 1 (a DWORD, a 32-bit registry number) to that value.

When a policy is set to Enabled, its explicit on-value and any on-value list are written. A list item uses its own registry key when it names one, else the list's default key, else the policy's key. Values marked delete are queued for deletion, numbers are saved as DWORD and text as strings.
When a policy is Enabled, an element is written only if the person supplied an option for it. Elements with no supplied option are left untouched.
When an Enabled policy has a decimal element, the number is saved as text if the element is defined to store as text. Otherwise it is saved as a DWORD.

When an Enabled policy has a checkbox element: checked with no defined on-value writes 1; unchecked with no defined off-value deletes the value. Otherwise the defined on or off value (or list) for the checkbox state is written.
When an Enabled policy has a text element, the text is saved as an expandable string if the element is defined as expandable, else as a plain string.

When an Enabled policy has a text-list element, existing values in its key are cleared first unless the element is defined to keep others. With no list supplied, the key is left cleared. Otherwise items are saved under names the person chose, or numbered 1, 2, 3 after the element's name prefix when it has one, else under the item text itself.
When an Enabled policy has a drop-down element, the chosen item's value and its value list are written. Multi-line text elements are saved as multi-string values.
When a policy is set to Disabled and defines no off-value, its registry value is deleted when it has a value name. Its explicit off-value and off-value list are written when defined.

When a policy is set to Disabled, every text-list element has its key cleared. A checkbox with a defined off-value or off-value list gets that off state written. All other elements have their value deleted.

A policy with no 'supported on' definition, or a blank one, counts as supported only when the caller allows unknown ('literal') support text. Entries naming no known product follow the same allowance.

A supported-on product entry is met when the computer's product list contains that product (unless the entry is a version range). A range applies only to a product with sub-versions: it is met when the computer has any sub-product, or its child, whose version lies between the range's minimum (default 0) and maximum (default highest known version).

A support definition combines its entries as 'any one' by default. 'All of' is honoured only when the caller asks for the any-logic option and the definition is marked All-of; then every entry, product or nested definition, must be met. Plain products are checked before nested definitions.
A support definition met again while it is being evaluated (a circular reference) counts as not met.
Registry keys and value names in a policy file are matched ignoring case; the first spelling met is kept and written back out.

When a policy (POL) file is opened, it is refused unless it starts with the 'PReg' signature, and refused when its format version is not 1. A value name may be followed by one extra empty character, which is tolerated.

When a POL file is opened, each record is kept under its key and value name; a later record with the same key and name replaces an earlier one. The record kinds (a plain value, a deletion marker or a key-clearing marker) set what state each value is in.
Same load rule, for the value state Queued for deletion: a '**del.' marker read from the file leaves the value queued for deletion.
Same load rule, for the state Key cleared: a '**delvals' marker read from the file leaves the key cleared.
Deleting a value in a POL file first forgets any value and marker for it. Unless it is already queued, a '**del.<name>' marker with the number 32 is then added, as Microsoft does.
Forgetting a value in a POL file removes both its value record and its deletion marker, so it returns to Not configured.
Setting a value in a POL file replaces any earlier record of the same value with the new data and kind. An existing deletion marker is not removed; the value record wins when the file is read.

A POL file value is queued for deletion when: it has a '**del.<name>' marker; its key has a key-clearing marker; its name is in the key's '**deletevalues' list (semicolon separated, ignoring case). A later real value record for it cancels this.
Listing the value names of a POL file key leaves out '**' marker names unless the caller asks for them.
When one POL file is applied to a target, a '**del.<name>' record deletes that value in the target.
When one POL file is applied to a target, a '**delvals' record clears all values of that key, and a '**deletevalues' record deletes each listed value, in the target.
When one POL file is applied to a target, a '**deletekeys' record clears each listed subkey in the target.
When one POL file is applied to a target, each ordinary value with a name is set in the target with its original spelling and kind. Other '**' records are ignored.

After applying a POL file against an older version, every value present in the old version but missing from the new one is forgotten in the target, but only if it lies under a policy branch (Software\Policies, Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies, System\CurrentControlSet\Policies).
Applying a POL file without an older version forgets nothing: every record is applied and no stale values are removed.
Clearing a key in a POL file forgets every value and marker in the key, and adds a '**delvals.' marker, so the key is in the state Key cleared.
Clearing a key in a POL file takes any value in it back to Not configured, because its records are forgotten.
Removing the key-clearing mark of a POL file key deletes every marker whose name starts with '**delvals' (with or without a final dot).
The sub-keys of a POL file key are listed once each, ignoring case, using the spelling first met; the key itself is never listed, and an empty key name means the root.
A text value stored in a POL file is read up to its first empty character. A multi-line value ends at the first empty line; kinds the program does not know are read as raw bytes.
When data is converted to POL storage, text kinds become two-byte characters ended by an empty character, and kinds not otherwise known are kept as raw bytes.
Deleting a value in the real Windows registry removes it when its key exists; a missing key or value is silently ignored.
Forgetting a value in the real Windows registry deletes it, because the registry cannot keep a value 'queued for deletion'.
Setting a value in the real registry creates the key if missing and stores the data; unsigned 32-bit and 64-bit numbers are saved as the same bits in signed form.
A registry value is reported present when its key exists and the value name matches ignoring case; an empty value name means the key itself and is present when the key exists.
Reading a registry value returns it without expanding %variables%, and numbers come back as unsigned; a missing key returns nothing.
The real registry never reports a value as queued for deletion.
A key path counts as a policy key when it equals, or lies below, one of Software\Policies, Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies or System\CurrentControlSet\Policies, ignoring case.
Clearing a key in the real registry deletes each value directly in the key; subkeys are untouched.
When a REG file is read, blank lines and lines starting with a semicolon are skipped.
A REG file is refused unless its first line is exactly 'Windows Registry Editor Version 5.00', with the message 'Incorrect REG signature'.
In a REG file a key header starting with '-' marks the whole key for removal; a value whose data is '-' marks that value for removal; '@' names the default value.

REG file data is read by its prefix: quoted text is a string, 'dword:' a hexadecimal 32-bit number, and 'hex' bytes of binary, or of the kind given in 'hex(n):' where n is hexadecimal. A line ending in a backslash continues on the next line.
A REG file value whose data matches none of the known forms is kept with no data and no kind.

When a REG file is written, a removed key is written as '[-name]', a removed value as 'name=-', an empty value name as '@', 32-bit numbers as 'dword:' with 8 hex digits, and other kinds as hex bytes, with 'hex(n)' for kinds other than binary and a line break after the position reaches 78 columns.
A key name from a REG file loses the chosen prefix (such as HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\) only when it begins with it, ignoring case; the prefix always ends with a backslash.
Keys in a REG file are matched by name ignoring case; value names too.
When a REG file is built from policy changes, writes to keys outside the chosen source branch are ignored; with no branch set, all are accepted. The branch itself and anything under it are accepted.
Setting a value in a REG file puts the key and value in the file, creating the key's record if no non-removal record exists, and replacing a same-named value, so the value is in the state Configured.
Deleting a value in a REG file does nothing if the key is already marked for removal. Otherwise the value is replaced by a removal mark, so it is in the state Queued for deletion.
Clearing a key in a REG file replaces the key's record, with all its values, by a whole-key removal mark, so the key is in the state Key cleared.
Forgetting a key clearance in a REG file removes the key's record only if it is a whole-key removal mark, returning it to Not configured. Normal keys are kept.
When a REG file is applied, a removed key clears that key in the target, a removed value deletes it, and every other value is set, using key names without the prefix.
A prefix for a REG file is guessed from the first key: for HKEY_USERS it includes the user's SID; otherwise it is the hive name; an empty file gives HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\.
A REG file contains default values when any value has an empty name.
Source branch given to a REG file has any trailing backslash trimmed.
A policy-state script (SPOL) that fails to load is reported with the parser's message plus '(Error found on line N.)'.
A SPOL script is refused unless its first line is 'Policy Plus Semantic Policy', with the message 'Incorrect signature.'
In a SPOL script a policy header starting with 'U' is a user-section policy; any other first letter is treated as computer section. The rest is the policy ID.

In a SPOL script an optional 'Comment:' line follows the header; '\\' stands for a backslash and '\n' for a line break. A backslash at the end of the comment, or followed by any other character, is refused ('Escape sequence started at end of comment.' / 'Unknown comment escape sequence').
A SPOL policy state must be 'Not Configured', 'Enabled' or 'Disabled' (any case); anything else is refused with 'Unknown policy state.'
Option lines in a SPOL script are read only for Enabled policies, until a blank line.

A SPOL option value is read as: '#n' signed integer; digits unsigned integer; true/false; 'text' in single quotes; "a", "b" list of strings; None an empty list; '[' block of one string per line (a list) or two (a name and value). An empty block means no list. Anything else is refused with 'Unknown option data format.'
When a SPOL script is written, the section letter is C for computer and U for user, followed by the policy ID.
A SPOL fragment writes a comment only when it is not empty, with backslashes doubled and line breaks as '\n'.
A SPOL fragment writes option lines only for Enabled policies; an Unknown state writes no state line.
SPOL options are written by type: integers with '#', unsigned numbers and booleans plain, text in single quotes, string arrays in double quotes (None when empty), lists as bracketed blocks.
When a SPOL script is applied, each policy goes to the computer or user source by its section, one failing policy is counted and the others continue; the failure count is returned.

When one SPOL policy is applied, its comment is saved only when comments are available and the comment is not empty; then any earlier state of the policy is forgotten before the new one is written. An unknown policy ID fails.

Group Policy tools are available only on Windows editions on the program's list of edition codes (Professional, Enterprise, Ultimate, Education and server and similar ones); Home and other editions are reported as without it.
A missing XML attribute, or one whose text cannot be converted to the default's type, reads as the default.
Two registry key/value pairs are the same when both key and value match ignoring upper or lower case.
A POL file is saved in sorted order of lowercase key and value name, so clearing and deletion markers ('**' names) come before ordinary values and are processed first.
A value in a POL file is reported as present only if it is not queued for deletion.
Asking for the data of a POL file value that is absent or queued for deletion returns nothing.
In a REG file, quotes and backslashes in value names and text data are written with a leading backslash.
When a REG file is read, a backslash in a value name or text data means the next character is taken literally and the backslash is dropped.

statement: Which Windows edition the computer is, and so whether Group Policy tools are offered, comes from a Windows system call. The code holds only a list of accepted edition codes, so new editions are missed until it is updated.

assumed.why: The edition code is returned by the operating system; the list's coverage of current Windows editions is not checkable from the code.
assumed.ifWrong: A supported edition is wrongly reported as lacking Group Policy, or an unsupported one passes.

evidence.shows: Edition code is read from Windows and compared to a fixed list.

says: A support definition already visited earlier in the same check counts as not met, even if it was met then and is not part of a circular reference. For an All-of definition, a shared sub-definition reached from two places therefore fails the whole definition the second time.

A plain supported-on product entry is met when the computer lists that product, or, for a parent product, when it lists any sub-product (or a sub-product's child). A version-range entry is met only by a sub-product, or its child, whose version lies within the range, minimum 0 and maximum the highest known version by default; listing the parent itself does not meet it. A product with no sub-products is met only by being listed. An entry with no known product is met only when unknown entries are approved.

A support definition is combined as All-of only when the caller opts in to honouring All-of and the definition is marked All-of; otherwise every definition is treated as any-one-of. An All-of definition is met when every entry is met, so one with no entries is met. An any-one-of definition is met when any entry is met, so one with no entries is not met. Products are checked before nested definitions.

When an Enabled policy has a text-list element that does not keep other values, the element's key is cleared first. With a list supplied, items are then saved under names the person chose, or numbered 1, 2, 3 after the element's name prefix when it has one, else under the item text itself. With no list supplied, the key is left cleared when the element does not keep others, and untouched when it does.
When an Enabled policy has a drop-down element, the chosen item's value is written and then the item's value list; both go under the element's key unless the item or its list names another key.
When an Enabled policy has a multi-line text element, the text is saved as a multi-string value.

Every on-value, off-value and value list written for a policy, a checkbox or a drop-down item (for Enabled and Disabled alike) follows one scheme. A list item uses its own registry key when it names one, else the list's default key, else the key of the policy or element that owns the list. A value marked delete is deleted, a number is saved as DWORD and text as a string; an absent value writes nothing.

Clearing a key in a POL file forgets the stored record of every value in it, so those values no longer hold data. The clearing marker it leaves makes every value in that key count as Queued for deletion, until a real value is set for it; they do not read as Not configured.

Applying a policy state to a SPOL script policy fails before anything else when the policy ID is unknown. Otherwise the comment is saved only when comments are available and the script's comment is not empty; an empty comment never erases an existing one. Any earlier state of the policy is then forgotten, so Not Configured is reached by that forgetting alone. If writing the new state then fails, the policy stays forgotten and its earlier state is lost.

Writing a policy state to a source decides only Enabled and Disabled. Not Configured and Unknown write nothing, so a caller must forget the policy's earlier values first for Not Configured to result. Enabled and Disabled writes do not remove stale values left by a previous state, apart from the deletes and clears the elements themselves make.

A REG file is only a write target. Setting a value, deleting a value, clearing a key and forgetting a key clearance work. Reading a value, checking a value, checking queued deletion, listing value names and forgetting a value are not implemented and fail. A difference-apply that must forget values fails if it targets a REG file, and a REG file cannot be read back as a policy source.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when an option line under an Enabled policy has no ': ' separator. The message is the system's own, not a Policy Plus text.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when the same option name appears twice under one policy.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when an option list opened with '[' is never closed with ']' before the text ends.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when a list entry holds no quoted text, or when entries after the first hold fewer strings than the first requires.
A SPOL script is refused, with the line number, when a policy header has no space between section and policy ID, or when the header is last in the text, or the state line is missing after it.

A REG file is only a write target. Setting a value, deleting a value, clearing a key and forgetting a key clearance work. Reading a value, checking a value, checking queued deletion, listing value names and forgetting a value are not implemented and fail. A difference-apply that must forget values fails if it targets a REG file, and a REG file cannot be read back as a policy source.

A REG file is only a write target. Setting a value, deleting a value, clearing a key and forgetting a key clearance work. Reading a value, checking a value, checking queued deletion, listing value names and forgetting a value are not implemented and fail. A difference-apply that must forget values fails if it targets a REG file, and a REG file cannot be read back as a policy source.
